<!-- The orientation workflow: consolidate the fortress-repo skill's revival part into a short orientation every worker reads whole, or update it after a landing from the FACTS the landing changed; how to run it and install its result. -->

# The orientation workflow

The `fortress-repo` skill's revival part, `references/revival-changes.md`, becomes the **orientation**: the short account of how revived Fortress departs from the original and from what a model expects, which every worker reads whole (Astra's review, `explorations/reviews/revival-record-synthesis.md`). `orientation.js` writes it, in two modes:

- **consolidate**, once, and again whenever the part has drifted: an outline by the concepts workers use and a table of where each old entry goes (`outline.md`); the writer writes the whole text from them; a preservation check against the table, a cold read with only the skill's core, and the regression quiz; the writer's fix round; a second cold read and the quiz again; a judge.
- **update**, after every landing: the landing's new and changed FACTS and POSITIONS entries pass the admission test (`admission.md`: the wrong default, the correction, the mistake it prevents); the writer rewrites the sections they touch in place, within the budget of 8K to 12K characters; the same checks, fix round, reread and judge.

The writer is a headless Opus stream (`../record-clarity/writer-stream.sh`), so its fix round resumes the session that wrote the text. The regression quiz is kept in `regression/` (questions and key), and grows with each update.

## Running it

    Workflow({ scriptPath: '/home/user/fortress/explorations/coordinator/tools/orientation/orientation.js',
               args: { mode: 'consolidate', out: '/abs/folder/', stream: 'orientation', concepts: ['/abs/concepts.md'] } })
    Workflow({ scriptPath: ..., args: { mode: 'update', out: '/abs/folder/', stream: 'orientation-bN', facts: ['F-261', 'P-153'] } })

## Installing its result

The judge writes `judgement.md` and `queue.md`. The coordinator then has the skill writer (`skill-writer.sh`) install the sections judged "install" into `references/revival-changes.md`, add `sources-mapping.md` to the skill's `references/sources.md`, and, after a consolidation, update the core's line for the part and its description together; then a cold read of the installed part, as `coordinator/references/skill-rewrite.md` says. Held sections keep the old text; their items go to `review-queue.md`.
export const meta = {
  name: 'orientation',
  description: 'The fortress-repo skill\'s orientation (its revival part): consolidate it whole, or update it from a landing\'s FACTS; outline or admission, the stream writer, preservation, cold read and regression quiz, a fix round, a second read, and a judge; nothing installed',
  phases: [
    { title: 'Plan', detail: 'consolidate: outline and disposition table; update: admission of the landing\'s findings', model: 'opus' },
    { title: 'Write', detail: 'the stream\'s headless Opus writer', model: 'opus' },
    { title: 'Check', detail: 'preservation, cold read, regression quiz', model: 'opus' },
    { title: 'Fix', detail: 'the writer\'s second round, in the same stream', model: 'opus' },
    { title: 'Reread', detail: 'a second cold read and the quiz again', model: 'opus' },
    { title: 'Judge', detail: 'install or hold, section by section, once', model: 'opus' },
  ],
}

// Temporary, for the week of the Fable 5.2 launch offer (the curator's order of 2026-11-10): every agent runs
// on Fable, at medium effort where it ran on Opus and at low effort where it ran on Sonnet. The phases above keep
// each role's usual tier. Set FABLE_WEEK to false to go back.
const FABLE_WEEK = false
const OPUS = FABLE_WEEK ? { model: 'fable', effort: 'medium' } : { model: 'opus' }
const SONNET = FABLE_WEEK ? { model: 'fable', effort: 'low' } : { model: 'sonnet' }

// args: { mode: 'consolidate' | 'update', out: '/abs/folder/', stream: 'name', concepts: ['/abs/concepts.md', ...] (consolidate),
//         facts: ['F-261', 'P-153', ...] (update: the FACTS and POSITIONS entries the landing added or changed) }
// Writes into out: outline.md and disposition.md, or admission.md; orientation.md and sources-mapping.md; the
// reports; judgement.md and queue.md. The coordinator installs a judged text through the skill writer.
const T = '/home/user/fortress/explorations/coordinator/tools/orientation/'
const RC = '/home/user/fortress/explorations/coordinator/tools/record-clarity/'
const MODE = args.mode
const OUT = args.out
const STREAM = args.stream || 'orientation'
const cut = (s, n) => (s ? String(s).slice(0, n) : null)
const ADMIT = { type: 'object', properties: { admitted: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' } }, summary: { type: 'string' } }, required: ['admitted', 'summary'] }

const drive = (n, task) => {
  const log = `${OUT}writer-${n}.log`, done = `${OUT}writer-${n}.done`
  return agent(`You drive a long command and report its output; you judge nothing and write nothing else. The folder ${OUT} may not exist yet: create it with mkdir -p.
1. If ${done} exists, skip to step 3.
2. Run this in the background with the Bash tool's run_in_background, exactly:
   ${RC}writer-stream.sh ${STREAM} "${task}" > ${log} 2>&1; touch ${done}
3. Run \`python3 ${RC}wait.py ${done} 540\` in the foreground, with a timeout of 600000 ms. If it exits 1, run it again; repeat until it exits 0.
4. Your final message: the last 60 lines of ${log}, verbatim.`, { label: n === 1 ? 'write' : 'fix', phase: n === 1 ? 'Write' : 'Fix', ...SONNET })
}

const quiz = async (round) => {
  if (round === 1) await agent(`Read your brief and follow it: ${T}quiz-author.md\n\nYour mode: ${MODE}. Your folder: ${OUT}`, { label: 'quiz author', phase: 'Check', ...OPUS })
  await agent(`Read your brief and follow it: ${T}quiz-reader.md\n\nThe orientation file: ${OUT}orientation.md\nThe cases file: ${OUT}quiz-cases.txt\nYour answers: ${OUT}quiz-answers-${round}.md`, { label: `quiz reader ${round}`, phase: round === 1 ? 'Check' : 'Reread', ...OPUS })
  return agent(`Read your brief and follow it: ${T}quiz-grade.md\n\nThe answers: ${OUT}quiz-answers-${round}.md\nYour grading: ${OUT}quiz-grade-${round}.md`, { label: `quiz grade ${round}`, phase: round === 1 ? 'Check' : 'Reread', ...OPUS })
}

phase('Plan')
let plan
if (MODE === 'consolidate') {
  plan = await agent(`Read your brief and follow it: ${T}outline.md\n\nYour folder: ${OUT}\nThe concepts lists: ${(args.concepts || []).join(', ')}`, { label: 'outline', phase: 'Plan', ...OPUS })
} else {
  const a = await agent(`Read your brief and follow it: ${T}admission.md\n\nYour folder: ${OUT}\nThe landing's FACTS and POSITIONS entries: ${(args.facts || []).join(', ')}`, { label: 'admission', phase: 'Plan', ...OPUS, schema: ADMIT })
  if (!a || !a.admitted.length) return { mode: MODE, admitted: [], summary: a ? a.summary : 'admission failed' }
  plan = a.summary
}

const W = `Read your brief and follow it: ${T}write.md. Your mode: ${MODE}. Your folder: ${OUT}`
const w1 = await drive(1, W)

const checks = await parallel([
  () => agent(`Read your brief and follow it: ${T}preserve.md\n\nYour mode: ${MODE}. Your folder: ${OUT}`, { label: 'preserve', phase: 'Check', ...OPUS }),
  () => agent(`Read your brief and follow it: ${T}coldread.md\n\nThe file to read: ${OUT}orientation.md\nYour report: ${OUT}cold-read.md`, { label: 'cold read', phase: 'Check', ...OPUS }),
  () => quiz(1),
])

const w2 = await drive(2, `${W}. This is your fix round: fix what ${OUT}preserve.md, ${OUT}cold-read.md and ${OUT}quiz-grade-1.md find, in ${OUT}orientation.md`)

const rereads = await parallel([
  () => agent(`Read your brief and follow it: ${T}coldread.md\n\nThe file to read: ${OUT}orientation.md\nYour report: ${OUT}cold-read-2.md`, { label: 'reread', phase: 'Reread', ...OPUS }),
  () => quiz(2),
])

const j = await agent(`Read your brief and follow it: ${T}judge.md\n\nYour mode: ${MODE}. Your folder: ${OUT}\nThe quiz gradings: ${OUT}quiz-grade-1.md, ${OUT}quiz-grade-2.md`, { label: 'judge', phase: 'Judge', ...OPUS })

return { mode: MODE, plan: cut(plan, 1200), write: cut(w1, 800), checks: checks.map(c => cut(c, 600)), fix: cut(w2, 800), rereads: rereads.map(c => cut(c, 600)), judge: cut(j, 1200) }
<!-- The orientation workflow's quiz reader: answer the regression questions with only the skill's core and the new orientation. -->

You are a new worker in the Fortress revival repository (`/home/user/fortress`). The grader compares each answer with its case below (`../quiz-grade.md`): **right**, **wrong**, or **right without its path or scope qualification**. Grade the decision and its scope, not the wording, and not whether the reader names the record entries. An answer that says "look it up first" is right only if it also says where, and what it does with each result the key names.

Each case gives:

- **Trap**: the default assumption that the case tests, and where it is on record: the pretraining quiz (`explorations/reviews/fortress-pretraining-quiz.md`, "the quiz"), its audit (`explorations/reviews/skills-distillation-audit.md`, "the audit"), or a worker's failure.
- **Expected**: the decision. **Scope**: the path and switch-over qualifications that a full answer needs.

usage: facts-extract.sh [--check] [--part N] [--page-bytes N] [--root DIR] [--common] [QUERY ...]

Prints what the queries name, whole and in the order they are given; a rung's
briefing is one such command. Each piece comes under a line naming its file
and section. The output comes in parts of at most PAGE_BYTES (default 28000);
part 1 opens with the size of the whole output in bytes and estimated tokens,
then what was asked for, where it is and what was not found; each part says
whether there is a next one, and --part N prints part N.

QUERY is one of:
  F-87, P-48             the entry of that number in FACTS.md or POSITIONS.md

  history:F-87           the entry's blocks in FACTS-history.md or

== explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md, ## Landed semantics

FACTS.md:286
- F-388 **The compiler's prelude declares its seven number types as value objects, whose classes the code generator writes over the run time's payload classes.** `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `RR32` and `RR64` are `value object`s in `CompilerBuiltin`; each object's class extends the abstract payload class `compiler/runtimeValues/F<T>`, which holds the JVM value. Descriptors, stamped instances and the RTTI's `className()` name the type by the payload class, while the RTTI's class stays the object's, so that the type lies below its traits at run time; a dotted call casts its receiver to the object's class; `F<T>.make` reaches the object's class's `make` by the name that `LibraryNames` gives, for the prelude only (the one library's seven have no rows yet, fork N4). So a program's object below a number type is refused at the compile, an overloading at `ZZ32` beside one at a program's trait is valid, a `typecase` clause at such a trait over a number is refused as unreachable (row 1081), and a number type named as a value does not compile (row 1082). Tests: `compiler_tests/NumberObjectsCompiled.test`, `compiler_tests/XXXNumberTypeExtendRefusedCompiled.test`, `compiler_tests/ComprisesMeetGenericTrait.test`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-number-payload-objects/REPORT.md`, "The design as built (a point to report)".

== explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md, ## The library's arrays and algebra

FACTS.md:305
- F-379 **The one library and walk declare `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN64` and `RR64` each as one value object, and a program's object below one is refused at load.** P-178's one-library half holds: the objects are `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:384`, `:846`, `:951`, `:1063`, `:1170`, and walk builds their native values from the glue classes of the same names, such as `interpreter/glue/prim/ZZ32.java`, found by a table (`interpreter/evaluator/BuildEnvironments.java:459-470`). No `Int`, `Long`, `Float`, `BigNum` or `UnsignedLong` is declared in the library or used by walk's Java; a typecase arm at one of those names is refused on both paths, 'Int is undefined.' (row 959, fixed; F-382). So `asif` at one of the five is the identity, and `object Mine extends ZZ32` is refused, 'Attempt to extend object type ZZ32'. Walk's load check reads pairs over the five as over objects: a valid generic-beside-plain pair at `ZZ64` loads (row 550, fixed), and so do two kinds of invalid pair: a plain declaration with no written return type beside a generic one (row 1044), and two plain lists whose more specific one returns a type not below the other's, against the Subtype Rule, such as `f(x: Number): ZZ32` beside `f(x: ZZ64): String` (row 697). With `NN32` and `RR32`, objects already, seven of the eight number types are objects, `QQ` the trait; the compiler's prelude declares the same seven as value objects (F-388). Tests: `tests/NumberTypesAreObjectsWalk.fss`, `tests/NumberTypeExtendRefusedWalk.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-number-objects/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why" and "What a program sees differently".

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### Numbers

POSITIONS.md:107
- P-178 **Each built-in number type is one `value object` under its own name, and walk's native number objects `Int`, `Long`, `Float`, `BigNum` and `UnsignedLong` go.** `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN64` and `RR64` are each declared `value object`, as `NN32` and `RR32` already are, in place of a trait with one native object below it, such as `trait ZZ32 comprises { Int }` with `value object Int extends ZZ32`. An object is a leaf, so no type of a program extends a built-in number type; a program's own number type extends `Number` (P-160). Compiled code can then hold a value of such a type as a bare JVM `int`, `long` or `double` (P-17), and both paths take this form before the switch-over: the one library by the merge, and the compiler's prelude by an exception to P-37, as for the numerals, which goes with the prelude. For the number types it replaces the pattern that P-164's reason names, a trait with walk's native object below it. Why: the two names are a duality between the two libraries, which the curator called a problem that the revival makes for itself by keeping it; the second names are walk's internals, which a program is not to see (P-167); and the compiler prelude's open trait let a program's object extend `ZZ32`, which a bare `int` cannot hold (row 866, such a program compiled and died when it ran). Detail: `reviews/carriers-ways-2026-11-13.md`, "Way D. One object per type: each number trait merged with its one object"; the merge as probed: `compile-ladder/plan-31/probes/number-object-merge.md`, "What was built".

The tree declares each a `value object` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:210`), whose class the code generator writes over the hand-written payload class `FZZ32`, now abstract over `FValue`. So on the compiled path a program's object below a number type is refused at the compile, 'Invalid type in extends clause: ZZ32' (`ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXNumberTypeExtendRefusedCompiled.test`); an overloading at `ZZ32` beside one at a program's trait is valid (`ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/OverloadZZ32BesideUserTraitCompiled.test`); a `typecase` clause at a program's trait over a `ZZ32` is refused as unreachable (`ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXTypecaseArmExcludedRefused.test`); and a static argument inferred from a number's run-time type names the class that compiled code names (`ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/ComprisesMeetGenericTrait.test`). ## Case 4: is a `ZZ32` a `ZZ64`; which overload runs; what a generic call promotes to

- **Trap.** A nested number tower (Java's widening, Haskell's classes; the audit, B.6, "missing"); Java's choice of `f(long)` for an `int` argument; no conversion at a generic call (Haskell), or `T` at the join `Number` (Julia).
- **Expected.**
  - `f(n)` gives `"number"`. `ZZ32` is not a subtype of `ZZ64`: the number types are siblings under `Number`. `f(x: Number)` fits the `ZZ32` argument without a conversion, and a conversion never changes which declaration runs when one already fits. The coercion from `ZZ32` into `ZZ64` is used only when no declaration fits without one.
  - `pick` runs, at `T = ZZ64`: the narrowest type into which both arguments coerce (promotion). The `ZZ32` argument is converted.
- **Scope.** Both paths give both answers. The compiled checker tries a call by subtyping before coercion and chooses the coercion statically; walk converts only when no declaration fits without conversion, and chooses by the run-time value. Walk promotes from run-time types, so where a static type is wider than its value the paths can instantiate differently (row 509), which this case does not reach.
- **Wrong.** `"wide"`; `pick` refused, or run at `Number`.
- **Partial.** Both answers right, with no reason given, or with `pick`'s instance explained as a subtype relation ("`ZZ32` widens to `ZZ64`") in place of a declared coercion.
- **Skill.** Core, "Numbers are siblings, not a tower"; the orientation's rules on the flat number types and on coercion and promotion.
- **Evidence.** P-43, P-46, P-49, P-74, F-131, F-128, F-137, F-73.

content.content:
## Setting up each call

Start every Bash call with these lines. They put you at the tree's root, where this skill's commands start unless they `cd`:

    cd <tree> && mkdir -p tmp
    export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64 PATH=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64/bin:$PATH
    export FORTRESS_HOME=$PWD FORTRESS_THREADS=1 TMPDIR=$PWD/tmp JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$PWD/tmp"
    unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS

- If `/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64` or `ant` is missing, run `apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y openjdk-25-jdk-headless ant` first.
- `bin/fortress` takes `FORTRESS_HOME` from the shell whenever it is set. If it names another tree, you run that tree's code. Check it with `echo $FORTRESS_HOME`.
- `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` is unset, because the proxy's trust-store flags in it break ant's JVM forks.

The lines give the settings of `explorations/experiment/env.sh`, with two differences:

- The JVM's temporary directory is your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
- They leave out env.sh's removal of old parser directories in `/tmp`, because your runs put theirs in your tree's `tmp/` (below).

If your brief tells you to run `source env.sh` and then to point `TMPDIR` and `JAVA_FLAGS` at `tmp/`, use the lines above. They do the same.

The library and microGPT import no DSL grammar, and of the gated tests only `ProjectFortress/syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss` does. The ungated tests beside it import one, and so do the APL experiments under `explorations/apl/`.

With the lines above, your runs that import a DSL grammar put their parser directories in `<tree>/tmp/`. Hundreds of them once filled the disk allowance. So:

- When no run of yours is live, remove yours: `rm -rf <tree>/tmp/fortress*rats`.
- Before a long run, check `df -h /`. How to read it: the `cloud-container` skill.

## The caches

All the caches are gitignored. A caches folder also holds:

- `environment_cache/`: another cache of walk's.
- `nativewrapper_cache/`: the wrappers for the Java classes that an api imports with `import java`.
- `global.map`: the linker's saved state, an empty map in practice. If it is missing, the linker writes an empty one, also in a private caches folder.
- `implementation.stamp`: the stamp of the build that the caches belong to ("Building", below).

Only these runs read `default_repository/caches`: `fortress compile`, `fortress run`, `fortress junit` (and `junit.sh`), `ant testOnly`, and a direct walk run. These runs use private caches (`-Dfortress.caches` and `FORTRESS_CACHES`), and need neither the library order nor warm caches: `harness-one.sh`, the gate's ladder regression (`gate.md`) and both ant suites. `harness-one.sh` keeps its private cache beside its scratch folder between calls (`tests-running.md`).

With `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`, a run that names no private caches folder uses `default_repository/caches-one` in place of `default_repository/caches`, because a caches folder holds the jars of a single library. Set the environment variable, not only the property `-Dfortress.library=one`. The class path scripts, `bin/fortress_classpath` and `bin/run_classpath`, read only the variable. With the property alone, the compile writes to `caches-one`, but the run looks in `caches` and prints 'Could not load P'. Run the library order without the variable: it fills `caches` with the prelude's jars. No compile writes the one library's jars yet, so a program compiled with the variable dies at its first library class: 'NoClassDefFoundError: fortress/FortressLibrary$String' (ledger row 1062).

## The `fortress` commands

`Shell.java` dispatches `bin/fortress <command>`.

- To see what an early phase makes of a program, stop after that phase: `parse` (a syntax check), `disambiguate`, `grammar`, `desugar` or `typecheck`.
- `unparse` prints the syntax tree back as Fortress source. Use it to see what a desugaring made.
- `link` links a compiled component (the `link` step of a compiled `.test` file). `api` writes a component's api. `test` runs a program's `test` declarations under walk.
- The command chooses the library. Walk and `test` call `Shell.useInterpreterLibraries()`. Every other command calls `useCompilerLibraries()`. Each call points `WellKnownNames` and `Types` to its prelude, and sets the desugaring switches. With `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`, `useCompilerLibraries()` points them to the one library (`Shell.java:377-388`).

## Running

    cd ProjectFortress
    # after an ant compileAll that started the caches again: the library order (build-and-caches.md)
    ../bin/fortress compile <path>/P.fss
    ../bin/fortress run P [args]

A small program compiles in about 5 s and runs in about 1 s.

- A crash of the checker prints one line and hides the Java stack. To see the stack, put `-debug stacktrace` before the file: `../bin/fortress compile -debug stacktrace <path>/P.fss`.
- A failed compile of a program leaves a 0-byte jar in `bytecode_cache/`. A run of the program then prints "Could not load P" and "Resource not found". Read the compile's error instead.

## One test, or a few

Each script and `fortress junit` below ends with the verdict of JUnit's text runner: `OK (n tests)`, or `FAILURES!!!` with the counts. Read the verdict there: the exit code is 0 whatever the verdict.

### Interpreter tests

Run interpreter tests (`ProjectFortress/tests/`) from the tree's root, after you set up the call:

    explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh <tree>/tmp/h1 \
        ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss [ProjectFortress/tests/X.test] [more files ...]

- It runs `SystemJUTest` with testSystem's JVM settings, at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, on a folder that holds only the files that you name.
- It keeps its cache in the folder `<scratch-dir>.cache`. It starts from that cache while the build and the library sources are those that filled it. Otherwise, or with `COLD_CACHE=1`, it starts empty. Its first line says `cache filled` or `cache empty`.
- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing. After you edit Java, Scala or a parser grammar, run `ant compileAll` first. If your tree has no build, seed it or build it as `worktrees.md` says.
- Give it a scratch directory that holds nothing else. The script deletes the directory when it starts and when it ends.
- If a test has an `X.test` file (its keys for a refusal at load), name it beside its `X.fss`.
- It takes 15 to 25 s with an empty cache, mostly to analyse the library, and about 4 s with a filled one. Name several files in one call to run them in one JVM.
- It shows the output of passing tests too, and removes the Java stack frames.

To see the whole diagnostic, with its Java stack, run the program directly, from `ProjectFortress/` as the harness does, because an import is looked up in the current directory first:

    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress -debug stacktrace tests/X.fss

The direct run and the harness use different heaps (`interpreter.md`, "Running a program").

### Compiled tests

Compiled tests are the `.test` files in `compiler_tests/`, `library_tests/` and `other_compiler_tests/`. They link with the library's jars in the tree's `default_repository/caches`. If a build started the caches again, or the tree's caches are empty, run the library order first (`build-and-caches.md`). The tests of `one_library_tests/` compile against the one library: run them with `ant testOneLibrary`.

The script is `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh`. `climb-batch-N` is the folder's real name, not a placeholder. Run your own tree's copy: it runs the tree that it is in.

    ONE_JVM=1 explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh <label> \
        ProjectFortress/compiler_tests X.test Y.test > <tree>/tmp/junit-<label>.txt 2>&1

- `<label>` is any word. It marks the run's lines in the output. The script writes to standard output only, so redirect it to your `tmp/`.
- With `ONE_JVM=1`, the whole list runs in one `fortress junit` run, in one JVM. The compile and link tests run before the run tests, as in the suite. Without `ONE_JVM=1`, each file gets its own JVM.
- It removes the named components' entries from the tree's `default_repository/caches` before the whole list and after it, not between files. So a link test and the run test that uses its jar pass in one call, with or without `ONE_JVM=1`.
- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing, as `harness-one.sh` does.
- It removes the Java stack frames, and cuts each line at 240 characters.
- Its JVMs keep their temporary files in the tree's `tmp/`, and run at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`.

To run the same list in one JVM without the script, and without its removal of cache entries:

    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress junit compiler_tests/X.test compiler_tests/Y.test

Run all the new files of one test folder together, in one JVM, as the suite does. A test that passes alone can fail beside others.

content.content:
The phases differ too: walk turns off some desugarings that the compiled path runs (`interpreter.md`, "Where a fix of walk belongs"). A fix of one of those desugarers changes only the compiled path.

## The compiler's prelude, until the switch-over

The compiled path uses the compiler's own prelude: `LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss`, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss` and `Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss`. With `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`, it uses the one library in their place. `Library/CompilerSystem.fss` is the compiled path's `System`.

Do not add a declaration to the three prelude files: the switch-over deletes them, and their tests stay. Two exceptions (P-37): its numeral types and coercions follow `revival-changes.md`, "Numbers", and a brief may ask to declare each built-in number type as one `value object`, the form that both libraries are to take. If a helper of `nativeHelpers/` that the one library binds is wrong, fix the helper's Java, even if the prelude binds it, and leave the prelude's text: its binding gives the fix. Change with it a compiled test that pinned the old result.

The class loader is code of this tree that the revival changes, so a failure while a class loads can be its defect (`references/compiler.md`).

HotSpot, the JVM's compiler, then compiles the hot bytecode to machine code. A number is a boxed object, also inside a specialised class: `RR64` is the class `FRR64`. An array is a library object, read and written through its `get` and `put` methods.

### The caches
21:- Values: walk's `interpreter/evaluator/values/` (`FInt`, `FFloat`), and the compiled `compiler/runtimeValues/` (`FZZ32`, `FRR64`).
22:- Number natives: walk's glue classes, in `interpreter/glue/prim/` (`ZZ32.java`, `ZZ64.java`).
34:Do not add a declaration to the three prelude files: the switch-over deletes them, and their tests stay. Two exceptions (P-37): its numeral types and coercions follow `revival-changes.md`, "Numbers", and a brief may ask to declare each built-in number type as one `value object`, the form that both libraries are to take. If a helper of `nativeHelpers/` that the one library binds is wrong, fix the helper's Java, even if the prelude binds it, and leave the prelude's text: its binding gives the fix. Change with it a compiled test that pinned the old result.
58:The compiler's prelude has no array types, only `ZZ32Vector` and `StringVector`. Its `for` loops, comprehensions and reductions work over `ZZ32` ranges only. Its reductions give a `ZZ32` or a `String`.
81:A body `builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.Class.method")` binds one such method, a helper, too. In a compile, at the parse, the compiled path, and not walk, rewrites the body as a call of the method through a generated `import java`, with `self` first in a trait or object (`compiler/BuiltinPrimitiveRewriter.java`). The checker then checks the declaration against the method's Java signature. In a compile, it reads `int` as `ZZ32`, `long` as `ZZ64`, `float` as `RR32`, `double` as `RR64`, `boolean` as `Boolean`, `String` as `JavaString`, `BigInteger` as `ZZ` and `Object` as `Any` (`NamingCzar.fortressTypeForForeignJavaType`). The compile stops in these cases:
109:  - an object whose one value parameter is a pair dies in its constructor with `ClassCastException` (ledger row 1055). Add a second value parameter beside the pair, as `object Holder(n: ZZ32, var pr: (ZZ32, ZZ32))`;
116:  - Until the switch-over, `RR64` converts only an `RR32` and a numeral, and `RR32` only a numeral. So a `ZZ32` value where an `RR64` is expected is refused (ledger row 442). Write `i.asRR64` for a `ZZ32` value `i`.
117:  - At a binding without a declared type, the checker refuses a `try` whose block and `catch` clause end in numerals, as `x = try 4 catch e Exception => 5 end`: 'NaturalNumeral cannot be written in a program except as a parameter's type.' (ledger row 1074). It also refuses a tuple binding to a `case` or a `try` whose branches are numeral tuples, as `(a, b) = case k of 1 => (1, 2) else => (3, 4) end`: 'Right-hand side has type OR(...), but left-hand side is a tuple of 2 variables.' (ledger row 1075). Declare the types, as `(a, b): (ZZ32, ZZ32) = case ...`.
120:  - As a `typecase`'s selector, a numeral keeps its own type, as `NaturalNumeral[\1,10,7\]`, so `typecase 7 of ZZ32 => ...` is refused as unreachable (ledger row 963). Bind the selector to a variable first, as `x = 7`, then write `typecase x of ...`.
121:  - A `label` block that ends in a numeral, where an `exit ... with` gives the block a `ZZ32` value, stops the code generator: 'Error trying to close method scope' (ledger row 340). Bind the numeral to a typed variable first, as `none: ZZ32 = -1`, and end the block with the variable.
126:- A reference to a generic function with one declaration, as `count[\F extends Object\](b: Box[\F\]): ZZ32`, takes its instance from the arrow type that receives it. Where the receiving type is not an arrow type, as in `p(count)` for `p(x: Any)`, the compile passes and the run dies with `NoClassDefFoundError` (ledger row 1012). Write the static argument there, as `p(count[\ZZ32\])`. The checker refuses a reference to a name with several declarations of which one is generic, unless one without static parameters fits the receiving arrow type (ledger row 1009). Pass a function of one declaration that calls the name.
128:- A `typecase` tuple pattern with an untyped binder, as `(x, y: ZZ32)`, stops the code generator: 'typcase match failure!' (ledger row 964). Walk stops on the same clause when it evaluates the `typecase`, with the same message. Give each binder a type.
136:  - a call of a functional method of an object that a trait's `comprises` clause lists, on a value whose static type is the object. An example is `num(R)`, where `trait Q comprises { R }` declares `abstract num(self): ZZ32` and `object R extends Q` gives its body. Call it through a value typed as the trait, as `q: Q = R` and then `num(q)` (ledger row 815);
137:  - a read of an exported object's value parameter, from a component that imports the api, where the exporting component names the parameter otherwise than the api. A value parameter is a parameter of the object's constructor, and also a field. An example is `Np(3).a`, where the api declares `object Np(a: ZZ32)` and the component `object Np(z: ZZ32)`. The export check compares no value parameter's name. Give each value parameter the api's name (ledger row 839);
